items.label: list_item
items.text: Stop heating the reaction mixture and allow it to cool slowly at room temperature so that larger crystals can form.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Remove the blue crystals from the reaction mixture by filtration, or by just pouring off the remaining solution.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The crystals can be dried by blotting them with a paper towel, or they can be left to dry in a warm place.

items.label: section_header
items.text: WHY NOT SIMPLY EVAPORATE THE SOLUTION TO DRYNESS?

items.label: text
items.text: It would seem much easier to just evaporate off all the water by boiling rather than crystallising the solution slowly, but evaporating to dryness wouldn't give you blue copper(Ill) sulfate crystals. Instead, you would produce a white powder of anhydrous copper(ll) sulfate.

items.label: text
items.text: When many salts form their crystals water from the solution becomes chemically bound up with the salt. This is called water of crystallisation. A salt which contains water of crystallisation is said to be hydrated. We can show the crystallisation part of the reaction as:

items.label: text
items.text: We can add excess magnesium to sulfuric acid. This time the acid does not have to be heated.

items.label: text
items.text: When we add the magnesium the reaction mixture will fizz (hydrogen is given off). We keep adding magnesium until the fizzing stops and there is magnesium left in the beaker. This means that all the acid has reacted. The equation for the formation of the solution of magnesium sulfate is:
